scenes.name: attainable performance and the roofline
scenes.visual: A log-log roofline plot for the H100. The horizontal axis represents arithmetic intensity in operations per byte; the vertical axis represents attainable throughput in operations per second. A slanted coral roof meets a flat amber ceiling at the ridge point: 295 operations per byte.

beats.say: Attainable performance is the absolute ceiling this chip could reach on a given algorithm. It is not a prediction; it is an upper bound.
beats.show: A log-log coordinate grid draws: x-axis 'Arithmetic intensity (ops/byte)', y-axis 'Attainable rate (ops/sec)'.

beats.say: Below the ridge, the slanted roof binds: the chip can do no more operations per second than memory bandwidth times arithmetic intensity.
beats.show: A slanted coral ceiling draws upward with slope equal to 3.35 TB/s: 'Memory-bound: rate = 3.35 TB/s × intensity'.

beats.say: Above the ridge, the flat ceiling binds: the tensor cores' peak of nine hundred and eighty-nine trillion operations a second.
beats.show: A flat amber ceiling draws horizontally at 989.4 TFLOP/s: 'Compute-bound: 989.4 TFLOP/s peak'.

beats.say: The inflection point where they meet is the ridge: nine hundred and eighty-nine trillion divided by three point three five trillion bytes, giving two hundred and ninety-five operations per byte.
beats.show: A vertical dashed line drops from the corner to 295 on the x-axis: 'Ridge = 295 ops/byte'. Takeaway: 'below 295 you wait on memory; above 295 you wait on arithmetic'.

scenes.name: prefill versus decode on the roofline
scenes.visual: The roofline diagram populated with prefill and decode phases. Decode lands far to the left at 1 op/byte in the memory-bound zone; prefill lands far to the right at 1,024 to 2,048 ops/byte in the compute-bound zone.

beats.say: Now place the two phases of running a language model onto that roofline.
beats.show: The H100 roofline remains in view with the 295 ridge marked clearly at center.

beats.say: Decode generates one token at a time, multiplying the token's vector by the weights. Each weight is read once, giving one operation per byte.
beats.show: A marker lands at 1.0 on the horizontal axis: 'Decode · 1 op/byte'. A vertical indicator shows it hitting the slanted memory roof, far below peak FLOPS.

beats.say: Prefill processes a whole prompt of thousands of tokens at once, reusing each weight thousands of times: one to two thousand operations per byte.
beats.show: A marker lands at 2,048 on the horizontal axis: 'Prefill · ~2,000 ops/byte'. An indicator shows it sitting firmly against the flat compute ceiling.

beats.say: The exact same model on the exact same hardware lives on opposite sides of the ridge: decode is starved for memory; prefill saturates the maths units.
beats.show: Arrows highlight the massive gulf between the two points. Takeaway pill: 'decode lives far left of the ridge; prefill lives far to the right'.

scenes.name: two real operations: array add versus matrix multiply
scenes.visual: A comparison of two fundamental mathematical operations against the H100 ridge: adding two arrays (0.17 ops/byte) versus multiplying two 1,024x1,024 matrices (341 ops/byte).

beats.say: Look at two basic mathematical operations to see how arithmetic intensity is set.
beats.show: Two algorithm cards appear: left 'Vector Addition: c[i] = a[i] + b[i]', right 'Matrix Multiply: C = A × B (1,024 × 1,024)'.

beats.say: Adding two arrays reads two numbers and writes one: six bytes of traffic for one addition, or zero point one seven operations per byte.
beats.show: Vector addition plots at 0.17 ops/byte on the roofline: deeply memory-bound, far below the ridge.

beats.say: Multiplying two thousand-by-thousand matrices performs over two billion operations on six megabytes of data: three hundred and forty-one operations per byte.
beats.show: Matrix multiplication plots at 341 ops/byte: crossing just to the right of the 295 ridge into compute-bound territory.

beats.say: They sit two thousand times apart, and neither number depends on the G P U. The chip sets the ridge; mathematics decides which side you land on.
beats.show: A bracket spans the 2,000× distance between the two algorithms. Takeaway pill: 'arithmetic intensity is a property of the algorithm, not the chip'.

checks.claim: Ridge: 989.4 TFLOP/s / 3.352 TB/s = 295.17 ops/byte, quoted as '295 operations per byte'
Vector addition intensity: 1 op / (3 numbers * 2 bytes) = 1 / 6 = 0.1667 ops/byte, quoted as '0.17 operations per byte'
1,024 x 1,024 matrix multiply intensity: 2 * 1,024^3 ops / (3 * 1,024^2 * 2 bytes) = 341.33 ops/byte, quoted as '341 operations per byte'
Ratio between matrix multiply and vector add intensity: 341.33 / 0.1667 = 2,048x, quoted as 'two thousand times apart'
